candidate.title: Erik Wielenberg vs Adam Lloyd Johnson — What Is the Best Account of Objective Morality? (2020)
candidate.label: Moral Foundations
candidate.motion: What is the best account of objective morality?
candidate.sourceNote: This assessment covers only the debaters’ direct exchange (approximately 33:05–1:13:25), as approved by the editor. The introductory position discussion, audience questions and all dependent answers, including the final reply to an audience question, are excluded. This recording has no separate formal opening speeches or paired closing statements. Neither speaker receives credit, penalties, or an inference of failing to reply from excluded material. These scores assess the direct exchange, not the complete recording. Source: the complete English automatic captions of the supplied September 27, 2020 recording, checked for coverage and speaker turns. No independent audio verification was completed because public audio retrieval failed. Uncertain caption wording is not treated as a speaker error. Featured quotations reproduce complete source statements; argument cards condense the eligible exchange.
candidate.scoringNote: Scores are AI-generated estimates of argumentative performance, rather than judgments about worldview truth; the separate AI Contribution does not affect these scores.

con.name: Objective morality needs no divine foundation
con.speaker: Erik Wielenberg

candidate.summary: Wielenberg’s focused parity, intrinsic-value, and obligation challenges outperformed Johnson’s theistic grounding, though Johnson pressed a serious evolutionary reliability problem.

pro.text: the ultimate good is what God is like.
pro.context: Johnson identifies God’s triune, loving character as the concrete ultimate reality that grounds goodness, rather than treating a moral proposition as independently fundamental.

con.text: a mother's love for her child is intrinsically good.
con.context: Wielenberg uses a concrete loving relationship to argue that moral value can belong to things themselves without requiring a separate Platonic object or divine source.

pro.words: Johnson makes God, rather than propositions about God, the ultimate reality and identifies God’s triune loving character as what humans recognize and call good.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson offers a clear ontological distinction between God as the concrete ultimate reality and propositions that merely describe God, thereby giving his grounding account a definite terminus rather than leaving it at an unexplained sentence or abstract rule. Principal limitation: Listing divine kindness, respect, care, and unselfishness does not explain why those traits are morally good; saying humans call them good risks relabeling the target property instead of grounding it, so Wielenberg’s specific challenge remains only partly answered. Live burden: Johnson must supply a non-circular bridge from God’s character to its normative value and show why a concrete bearer explains goodness better than Wielenberg’s fundamental moral truths. Locked score: 68 recognizes a relevant and intelligible reply with good clarity, while its decisive value-grounding inference receives limited warrant.

con.words: Wielenberg argues that calling Trinitarian love good may itself be a foundational moral axiom, so divine grounding does not automatically improve on non-theistic moral foundations.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg isolates the precise comparison the motion requires by distinguishing the loving relation from the further proposition that this relation is good, then arguing that an unexplained goodness claim would leave theism and non-theistic realism with structurally similar foundations. Principal limitation: The parity result depends on showing that Johnson cannot ground goodness in God’s concrete character, and this opening challenge poses that question rather than independently demonstrating that every divine-character account must contain an ungrounded moral axiom. Live burden: Johnson must explain why the ultimate being’s loving traits possess moral value without merely redescribing them as kind, caring, respectful, and unselfish, while Wielenberg retains responsibility for defending the claimed symmetry. Locked score: 84 reflects a highly precise, charitable, motion-level challenge whose central premise remains disputed rather than established.

pro.words: Johnson compares ultimate stopping points and demands positive reasons for Wielenberg’s basic moral axioms, contrasting their asserted fundamentality with arguments offered for God.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson correctly insists that identifying a proposition as fundamental does not establish its truth and frames a comparative question about which proposed stopping point has stronger reasons and explanatory support. Principal limitation: He names teleological and cosmological arguments without developing them inside the assessed exchange, so the claimed evidential advantage for God is only sketched, while describing Wielenberg’s axioms as merely proposed understates the abductive defense Wielenberg offers. Live burden: Wielenberg must give affirmative grounds for positing necessary moral truths, but Johnson still bears the parallel burden of showing that his cited arguments support the particular triune, morally perfect ground his account requires. Locked score: 79 rewards a coherent, central, and clearly expressed demand for comparative support, with deductions for its undeveloped pro-side evidence and slight overstatement.

con.words: Wielenberg argues abductively for basic moral axioms and conditionally claims that, if theistic morality also contains them, objective morality leaves both accounts on equal footing.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg gives a route from the apparent reality of objective morality to basic axioms and, crucially, states that the parity argument depends on the unresolved premise that Johnson’s theory also contains foundational moral claims. Principal limitation: Invoking inference to the best explanation supplies little comparison among candidate explanations, and the dilemma between accepting axioms and abandoning objectivity works only if that disputed premise succeeds rather than repeated assertion. Live burden: Wielenberg must show why basic truths explain objective morality better than rival grounds and establish the conditional parity premise; Johnson can resist the conclusion by completing his account of divine goodness rather than disproving moral realism. Locked score: 74 credits careful qualification, strong relevance, and useful responsiveness while reflecting limited warrant for the abductive preference and conditional dilemma.

pro.words: Johnson argues that abstract moral entities are inadequate stopping points because they require explanation, and he suggests a divine source offers the deeper account they need.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson presses a legitimate explanatory question about why apparently abstract moral truths should be treated as ultimate and asks whether Wielenberg’s moral realism depends on the controversial ontology of separate Platonic entities. Principal limitation: The move slides among moral truths, brute facts, properties, and abstract objects, relies on undeveloped historical references, and infers that God is probably their source without explaining why a divine mind is a better terminus than the entities themselves. Live burden: Johnson must first establish that Platonism is essential to Wielenberg’s account and then supply the inference from explanatory need to God; Wielenberg may answer the narrower objection by separating concrete property-bearers from optional abstract universals. Locked score: 63 reflects a relevant and responsive metaphysical challenge whose target and theistic conclusion remain insufficiently established.

con.words: Wielenberg separates concrete things bearing moral properties from optional abstract universals, arguing that intrinsic goodness survives regardless of how the independent Platonism dispute is resolved.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg directly undercuts Johnson’s chosen target by distinguishing concrete bearers of moral features from separate abstract property entities and candidly allowing that his moral realism can abandon Platonism if the independent universals debate goes against it. Principal limitation: Removing abstract objects does not explain why concrete relations possess unsourced moral properties, and the bottle and number analogies clarify the ontological distinction without providing new warrant for the mother’s love being intrinsically good. Live burden: Wielenberg must still defend fundamental moral features in concrete reality, but Johnson cannot treat an optional abstract-object ontology as a necessary defect or infer God merely from its explanatory demands. Locked score: 81 rewards a precise, charitable, and highly responsive clarification that defeats the specific objection while leaving the deeper grounding question open.

pro.words: Johnson asks Wielenberg to define non-natural moral properties and address the concern that their departure from physicalism makes the account controversial among atheists.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson asks two diagnostic questions that force Wielenberg to specify what kind of reality moral properties occupy and to acknowledge that atheism alone does not entail acceptance of his non-natural ontology. Principal limitation: Resistance from physicalist atheists is sociological pressure rather than evidence that non-natural moral properties are false, and the challenge supplies no argument establishing either physicalism or the breadth and force of that constituency objection. Live burden: Wielenberg must explain the positive content of non-naturalness and why irreducible moral properties are preferable to physical reduction, while Johnson would need a truth-relevant objection rather than mere discomfort to turn clarification into a comparative advantage. Locked score: 76 rewards the clear and responsive request for ontological detail but reflects its modest evidential support and partly peripheral popularity concern.

con.words: Wielenberg defines moral properties as real yet nonphysical, reasoning that wrongness differs categorically from measurable features and therefore belongs to a fundamental non-natural domain.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg directly defines non-naturalism, carefully separates science from scientism, and explains through the contrast between wrongness and properties such as mass or volume why objective morality may be real without being physically measurable. Principal limitation: The argument moves largely from moral appearance and the asserted implausibility of physical reduction to a separate fundamental category, without testing sophisticated reductionist alternatives or showing that failure of present empirical access establishes irreducibility. Live burden: Wielenberg must strengthen the inference from apparently nonphysical moral features to genuinely fundamental properties, whereas Johnson cannot defeat the account merely by noting that physicalist atheists reject it. Locked score: 81 reflects exceptional responsiveness, precision, and relevance to the motion, tempered by an intuitive evidential base and an underdeveloped elimination of competing ontologies.

pro.words: Johnson grants the Godless hypothetical for argument and says evolutionary selection would explain motherly love as survival-enhancing subjective feeling rather than independent objective value.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson eventually accepts Wielenberg’s counterfactual for argument and offers an evolutionary mechanism explaining why caregivers with loving dispositions would protect offspring, survive, and reproduce more successfully than indifferent alternatives. Principal limitation: A causal account of how loving feelings or behavior arose does not show that the resulting relationship lacks objective value, so the reply conflates the origin of a disposition with the truth or ground of a moral property and never excludes their compatibility. Live burden: Johnson must provide the missing inference from evolutionary selection to subjectivity or explain why divine creation uniquely confers value; Wielenberg need not produce a complete alternative worldview merely because he identifies that gap. Locked score: 56 reflects an understandable and relevant alternative explanation whose central category shift limits coherence, responsiveness, and charity.

con.words: Wielenberg presents a mother’s love for her baby as value contained in the relationship itself and asks whether Johnson must deny that value without God.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg turns the abstract grounding dispute into a concrete counterexample, defines intrinsic value as value not derived from an external source, and asks Johnson to confront the exact implication of claiming that all goodness depends on a triune God. Principal limitation: The mother-and-child case makes intrinsic goodness intuitive but does not independently establish that the relation’s value is metaphysically self-contained, so the example risks relying on moral appearance that the grounding dispute is meant to explain. Live burden: Johnson must address whether an evolutionary cause of loving feelings excludes objective value in the relation, while Wielenberg must defend the inference from evident goodness to independence from external grounding. Locked score: 82 recognizes a precise, relevant, and charitable challenge with substantial intuitive force, while preserving the unresolved metaphysical step.

pro.words: Johnson accepts that goodness and duty differ, illustrates supererogatory goodness with an orphanage, then links good obedience to loving God and resembling Trinitarian love.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson explicitly accepts Wielenberg’s value-duty distinction and illustrates it effectively with a morally good orphanage project that is not obligatory, showing that he understands the precise conceptual problem his theory must solve. Principal limitation: His proposed endpoint again establishes that obedience is good because it resembles and expresses divine love, but it never identifies what makes that good act required, effectively restating the premise Wielenberg had already shown insufficient for mustness. Live burden: Johnson must add a principle connecting created persons, divine relationship, or authority to binding duty without assuming the obligation under explanation; Wielenberg need only sustain the exposed gap. Locked score: 60 gives credit for clarity, concession, and relevant engagement, while the unanswered central question substantially lowers coherence and responsiveness.

con.words: Wielenberg distinguishes moral value from obligatory mustness and argues that showing obedience resembles divine goodness does not explain why obedience is required.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg identifies the missing inference in Johnson’s account: resemblance to a good exemplar may explain why obedience is valuable, but goodness alone does not entail the mustness that constitutes obligation. Principal limitation: Because the move is a diagnostic challenge, it does not itself provide Wielenberg’s rival theory of obligation or prove that no personal relationship could generate duties, although neither task is required for the objection to succeed. Live burden: Johnson must identify what converts loving resemblance into a binding requirement, while Wielenberg’s narrower burden is to maintain the conceptual distinction rather than establish an entire non-theistic moral system within this question. Locked score: 90 reflects exceptional coherence, precision, charity, and direct contact with the obligation burden, with only the inherent incompleteness of a targeted challenge.

pro.words: Johnson says created loving purpose generates human obligations, while God’s role as moral judge supplies accountability and punishment rather than serving as duty’s sole source.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson answers directly by distinguishing one reading on which God’s creative purpose for humans to love God and others grounds duty from the separate claim that God judges people and supplies accountability for violations. Principal limitation: The response largely asserts that being created for a purpose generates binding duties and does not explain why a creator’s intention has normative authority over persons, leaving the transition from intended function to moral mustness underwarranted. Live burden: Johnson must defend that authority bridge without collapsing obligation into obedience or enforcement, while Wielenberg would need further argument to show that created relational purpose could never contribute to duty. Locked score: 79 rewards the structure and strong responsiveness of this clarification, with deductions because the proposed purpose-to-obligation connection remains the decisive unsupported step.

con.words: Wielenberg quotes Johnson’s link between guilt and personal authority, then asks whether punishment or getting in trouble is necessary for a moral obligation to exist.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg grounds his question in a specific formulation from Johnson and sharply separates the existence of a duty from guilt, punishment, or other consequences for violating it, exposing a possible conflation without presuming that Johnson endorses it. Principal limitation: The move remains primarily clarificatory and therefore does not establish that accountability is irrelevant to every theory of obligation or present Wielenberg’s own full explanation of obligatory force, though it need not do so to frame the issue. Live burden: Johnson must assign distinct explanatory roles to what creates duty and what enforces it; Wielenberg bears only the focused burden of showing why consequences are not constitutive of obligation. Locked score: 86 reflects excellent precision, charity, responsiveness, and concrete support, moderated by the deliberately diagnostic scope of the contribution.

sections.title: Evolution and access to moral truth

pro.words: Johnson argues that unguided evolutionary contingency could have produced very different moral beliefs, leaving their alignment with independent necessary moral truths in need of explanation.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Johnson identifies a genuine epistemic challenge by separating independently existing moral truths from beliefs shaped by unguided evolution and asking what explains enough correspondence for humans to possess reliable moral knowledge. Principal limitation: The objection characterizes evolution as haphazard and invokes divergent possible paths only generally, without considering directional selection, cultural correction, or reasoning mechanisms that might reduce the alleged coincidence, so its evidential force remains suggestive rather than measured. Live burden: Wielenberg must explain truth-tracking rather than merely the usefulness of moral beliefs, while Johnson must show that theism actually predicts reliable access rather than simply announcing divine guidance as an available explanation. Locked score: 81 reflects a coherent, central, and clearly targeted challenge with strong burden contact, tempered by limited development and somewhat overstated evolutionary randomness.

con.words: Wielenberg concedes imperfect alignment, fixes necessary truths on one side, and explains partial convergence through selected self-concern plus similarity-based generalization to others.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Wielenberg acknowledges imperfect moral agreement and theism’s explanatory advantage, then supplies a two-stage mechanism in which survival favors recognizing one’s own pain and rights while similarity reasoning extends status to others. Principal limitation: The necessity of moral truths removes variation on the truth side but does not make beliefs track them, and although he says recognizing others’ pain and rights is probable and that the process heads toward truth, his claim that generalization inevitably identifies relevant similarity remains too confident. Live burden: Wielenberg must show that selection and reasoning yield truth-sensitive reliability beyond self-protection, while Johnson must not treat every imperfect or natural process as incapable of knowledge. Locked score: 77 rewards exceptional responsiveness, relevant mechanism-building, and concessions, with deductions for limited warrant and the overconfident inevitability claim.

strengths: Johnson consistently forced a comparison between rival ultimate stopping points and demanded positive support for Wielenberg’s foundational moral truths.
His lucky-coincidence objection clearly exposed the epistemic gap between independently necessary moral facts and beliefs shaped through unguided evolutionary history.
He distinguished created loving purpose from divine judgment, directly answering the concern that punishment alone generates moral obligation.

blunders.text: The evolutionary explanation of motherly love addressed the origin of feelings but did not show that the loving relation lacks objective value.
His resemblance account repeatedly explained why obedience is good while leaving Wielenberg’s specific question about obligatory mustness unanswered.

strengths: Wielenberg’s axiom-parity challenge precisely targeted whether divine grounding actually escapes the foundational stopping point attributed to non-theistic realism.
He separated value from obligation with unusual clarity and exposed the missing inference from good resemblance to binding requirement.
His responses directly defined non-natural properties, made Platonism optional, and offered a concrete mechanism for limited evolutionary convergence.

blunders.text: His abductive defense of basic moral axioms remained thin and depended heavily on the disputed claim that every objective theory contains them.

The evolutionary reply preserved a useful probability qualification about recognizing others’ pain and rights, but overstated that generalization inevitably identifies relevant similarity on the way toward moral truth.

finalArgument.thesis: A personal divine ground best explains why objective moral value binds created persons and why their moral cognition can answer to that value.
premises: Objective morality includes value, binding requirements, and a credible relation between moral truths and the cognitive agents expected to recognize them.
Purely fundamental properties can describe which acts are good or wrong without yet explaining why those truths address particular persons as duties.
If persons are intentionally created for loving relationships, their capacities and purposes can be jointly ordered toward truths grounded in the creator’s stable character.
A morally perfect creator can connect value, authority, and epistemic access without making punishment the source of obligation or treating evolved cognition as accidental.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, if the divine character-to-goodness and created-purpose-to-duty bridges are independently defended, theism offers a unified explanation that fundamental moral properties alone do not yet supply.

newArguments.title: Authority Without Threat
newArguments.text: Created purpose supplies practical authority when it is joined to perfect knowledge of each person’s flourishing and requirements consistent with that good, rather than resting on ownership or threatened punishment. A perfectly good creator brings persons into relationships for which reciprocal love is constitutive of flourishing and gives them capacities suited to those relationships. Judgment then responds to duties already grounded in that justified relation; it does not manufacture obligation. Divine purpose can therefore connect value with authority only if the creator’s intentions are themselves shown to serve the creature’s good.

newArguments.title: Integrated Reliability
newArguments.text: A theistic account predicts a fallible but corrigible moral faculty if rational and social capacities are intended to recognize basic goods while evolutionary development and cultural learning introduce predictable distortion. Moral disagreement is compatible with that design because self-interest can obstruct capacities that remain capable of correction. Systematic convergence under reflection would nevertheless count as evidence that those capacities answer to a common moral order. The comparison turns on which view better predicts both persistent bias and the possibility of principled correction, rather than on whether either view guarantees perfect moral agreement.

finalArgument.thesis: Objective moral features can be fundamental aspects of concrete relations, generate reasons through their evaluative structure, and become partly knowable through ordinary cognition.
premises: Some concrete relations present stable value-making features, such as attentive care that protects another person’s flourishing without exploitation or coercion.
Recognizing those features supplies agent-neutral reasons because relevantly similar interests count similarly unless a morally relevant difference justifies unequal treatment.
Neither the existence of such reasons nor their binding force logically requires punishment, divine command, or a separate abstract universal.
Evolution can favor sensitivity to pain, cooperation, and similarity while reflective reasoning corrects parochial extensions and tests principles for consistency.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, non-theistic realism can connect concrete value, obligation, and limited moral knowledge if it explains reason-giving features and corrigible generalization more fully than the live exchange did.

newArguments.title: Reasons From Relations
newArguments.text: Concrete relations generate obligation through the reasons their evaluative features give agents. Severe avoidable suffering supplies a reason against causing it, and an agent’s unique ability to prevent that suffering at trivial cost strengthens the reason until contrary considerations cannot reasonably defeat it. Obligation arises from the structure and weight of those reasons rather than from the prospect of punishment. This account preserves the distinction between goodness and duty while explaining how situational facts about harm, agency, cost, and alternatives can convert objective value into a binding requirement.

newArguments.title: Error-Correcting Convergence
newArguments.text: Evolutionary convergence is credible when generalization remains corrigible rather than inevitable. Selection can produce self-concern and limited cooperation, while language, perspective-taking, and consistency testing allow communities to expose arbitrary exclusions. A principle protecting one person’s pain loses coherence when it cannot survive application to relevantly similar others, so revision can extend concern without guaranteeing universal success. The resulting mechanism predicts persistent error alongside partial convergence and explains a route toward truth without claiming that survival selection directly tracks every independent moral fact.

noveltyMap.explanation: This unifies Johnson’s separate grounding, obligation, and knowledge claims while adding explicit bridge conditions that prevent divine character and created purpose from functioning as unsupported labels.
This adds a non-punitive account of justified divine authority and directly repairs the live exchange’s failure to derive mustness from goodness or created purpose.
This turns the reliability objection into a comparative prediction about fallibility, bias, and correction rather than assuming that divine guidance entails accurate moral belief.
This connects Wielenberg’s separate claims about intrinsic value, obligatory force, and epistemic access through a reasons-based structure absent from his direct answers.
This supplies a positive explanation of obligation through sufficiently weighty reasons, extending beyond the debate’s successful diagnosis that value and punishment do not themselves create duty.
This replaces the overstated inevitability claim with an error-correcting social mechanism that predicts both continuing disagreement and principled expansion beyond evolved self-interest.
